bracket: [Textbook inconsistency in the book's own worked solution: it computes "Change in potential energy \(= -3\,\text{J} - (-6\,\text{J}) = 3\,\text{J}\)" — which is a RISE, from \(-6\,\text{J}\) to \(-3\,\text{J}\) — and then asserts in the next breath that "there is loss in potential energy". Both halves describe real but DIFFERENT stages: when the field turns through \(60^\circ\) the potential energy rises to \(-3\,\text{J}\); the dipoles then re-align with the new field direction, carrying it back to \(-6\,\text{J}\), and THAT \(3\,\text{J}\) loss is the heat the question asks for. The final answer is correct; only the labelling runs the two stages together.]
